title: Sorting with Comparators
summary: Sort pairs, intervals, objects, and map entries by one or more keys, and write comparators for orders you define yourself.
intro: Interview problems sort all the time: intervals by start, words by count, cards by suit. You already know `sort((a, b) => a - b)` and `localeCompare`. Here you sort arrays of pairs by a column, objects and map entries by several keys, and data in an order you define yourself.

steps.title: Pairs and intervals by a column
steps.body:
When each item is an array, such as `[start, end]`, the comparator receives two whole items. Subtract the column you want to sort by:

```javascript
const meetings = [[9, 10], [1, 3], [4, 8]];
meetings.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]); // by start
console.log(JSON.stringify(meetings)); // [[1,3],[4,8],[9,10]]
```

Use `a[1] - b[1]` for the second column, and swap the sides, `b[0] - a[0]`, to sort high to low. For a tie-break, chain a second rule with `||`. A tie gives `0`, which is falsy, so `||` moves on to the next rule:

```javascript harness
const pairs = [[2, 5], [1, 9], [2, 1], [1, 3]];
{{code}}
console.log(JSON.stringify(pairs));
```

```javascript
pairs.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0] || b[1] - a[1]); // first column up, then second column down
```

Once intervals are sorted by start, an overlap shows up between neighbors: interval `i` overlaps the one before it when it starts before that one ends.

**The gotcha:** `sort()` with no comparator turns each pair into a string such as `"10,1"`, so `[[10, 1], [9, 2]].sort()` leaves them in that order, because `"1"` comes before `"9"`. Always pass a comparator for arrays of arrays.

example.title: Meeting schedule
example.prompt: Read meetings as `name start end`, sort them by start time (ties by end time), print the schedule, then print each clash between neighbors.
example.stdin:
review 13 15
standup 9 10
lunch 12 13
planning 10 12
design 14 16
sync 9 11
example.output:
9-10 standup
9-11 sync
10-12 planning
12-13 lunch
13-15 review
14-16 design
clash: standup and sync
clash: sync and planning
clash: review and design
example.explanation: Each meeting becomes `[name, start, end]`, so the comparator reads column 1 for the start and column 2 for the end. `standup` and `sync` both start at 9, and `|| a[2] - b[2]` puts the one that ends first ahead. After sorting, the second loop only compares each meeting with the one before it: `[prevName, , prevEnd]` skips the start it doesn't need. `lunch` starts at 12 exactly when `planning` ends, and `12 < 12` is false, so touching meetings don't clash.

practice.title: Free time between bookings
practice.prompt:
Read room bookings as `name start end`, sort them, and print the free gaps.

1. Sort by start time. When two bookings start together, put the one that ends later first.
2. Print each booking as `start-end name`.
3. Walk the sorted bookings keeping `latestEnd`, the latest end time so far (start it at the first booking's end). When a booking starts after `latestEnd`, print `free latestEnd-start`. Then raise `latestEnd` if this booking ends later.
4. If there was no gap at all, print `fully booked`.

Input:

```text
art 14 16
yoga 8 10
chess 10 11
band 8 12
drama 15 17
choir 18 20
```

Expected output:

```text
8-12 band
8-10 yoga
10-11 chess
14-16 art
15-17 drama
18-20 choir
free 12-14
free 17-18
```

tests.stdin:
art 14 16
yoga 8 10
chess 10 11
band 8 12
drama 15 17
choir 18 20
tests.output:
8-12 band
8-10 yoga
10-11 chess
14-16 art
15-17 drama
18-20 choir
free 12-14
free 17-18

hints: The start is column 1 and the end is column 2. For the tie-break, the later end goes first, so subtract the other way round: `b[2] - a[2]`.
A booking that starts inside a long earlier one is not free time, which is why you compare with `latestEnd` and not just the previous booking's end.
Count the gaps you print, and after the loop print `fully booked` when the count is still 0.

steps.title: Objects and map entries by several keys

example.title: Top words
example.prompt: Count the words in some text, sort them by count (highest first, ties A to Z), and print the top 3.
example.stdin:
the quick fox and the lazy dog
the dog and the fox
example.explanation: `[...counts]` turns the Map into pairs such as `["the", 4]`. The comparator puts higher counts first with `b[1] - a[1]`, and the three words with 2 tie, so `localeCompare` orders them alphabetically. `slice(0, 3)` keeps the first three pairs, which destructure into `word` and `count`.

practice.title: Leaderboard
practice.prompt:
Read game results as `name points` (a player can appear many times) and print a ranked leaderboard.

1. Total each player's points in a Map.
2. Turn the Map into an array of objects `{ name, total }`.
3. Sort the objects by `total`, highest first, and players with the same total by name A to Z.
4. Print each as `rank. name total`, starting at rank 1.

Input:

```text
ann 40
bo 70
cy 50
ann 30
dee 20
cy 20
bo 5
```

Expected output:

```text
1. bo 75
2. ann 70
3. cy 70
4. dee 20
```

tests.stdin:
ann 40
bo 70
cy 50
ann 30
dee 20
cy 20
bo 5

hints: Total with `totals.set(name, (totals.get(name) ?? 0) + points)`, the same pattern as counting.
`[...totals].map(([name, total]) => ({ name, total }))` makes the objects. The parentheses around the object tell JavaScript it isn't a function body.
Sort with `b.total - a.total`, then `|| a.name.localeCompare(b.name)` for ties.

steps.title: Orders you define yourself

example.title: Task board
example.prompt: Read tasks as `priority day name`, sort them by priority (high, medium, low), then by day, then by name, and print the board.
example.stdin:
low 3 water plants
high 2 fix login
medium 1 write docs
high 1 deploy
low 1 tidy desk
medium 1 review
example.output:
[high] day 1: deploy
[high] day 2: fix login
[medium] day 1: review
[medium] day 1: write docs
[low] day 1: tidy desk
[low] day 3: water plants
example.explanation: `...words` gathers the rest of the line, so names with spaces survive, and `join(" ")` puts them back together. `rank.get` turns each priority into 0, 1, or 2, so subtracting puts `high` first. The two `medium` tasks on day 1 tie on both numbers, and `localeCompare` puts `review` before `write docs`.

practice.title: Sorting a hand of cards
practice.prompt:
Read a hand of cards such as `10H QS 3D` (the rank, then one letter for the suit) and print it sorted.

1. Sort by suit in the order spades `S`, hearts `H`, diamonds `D`, clubs `C`. Give each suit its place in a Map.
2. Within a suit, sort by rank from high to low. Number cards are worth their number, and `faceValue` gives `J`, `Q`, `K`, and `A`.
3. Print the sorted cards joined by spaces.

`card.at(-1)` is the suit and `card.slice(0, -1)` is the rank.

Input:

```text
10H QS 3D AH 10S 2C KD
```

Expected output:

```text
QS 10S AH 10H KD 3D 2C
```
hints: `new Map([["S", 0], ["H", 1], ["D", 2], ["C", 3]])` gives each suit its place, so `suitRank.get(a.at(-1)) - suitRank.get(b.at(-1))` sorts by suit.
For the rank, `faceValue.get(rank) ?? Number(rank)` uses the face value when there is one and the number otherwise.
High to low means `value(b) - value(a)`, chained after the suit rule with `||`.

recap:
- A comparator returns a negative number when `a` goes first, a positive number when `b` goes first, and `0` for a tie.
- Sort arrays of pairs by a column: `(a, b) => a[0] - b[0]`, or `b[0] - a[0]` for high to low.
- Chain tie-breaks with `||`, most important rule first: `a[0] - b[0] || b[1] - a[1]`.
- `sort()` with no comparator compares pairs as strings, so always pass one.
- Objects compare fields: numbers subtract, strings use `localeCompare`.
- Spread a Map into `[key, value]` pairs with `[...map]`, then sort by `[1]` for the value and `[0]` for the key.
- For a custom order, map each value to a number (a rank Map or a key function) and subtract.
- Sorting is stable: items that tie on every rule keep their input order.
